title: Paying BRAC's Teachers for What Mothers Remembered
dek: From 1980 BRAC taught mothers house by house to make oral rehydration solution, and Fazle Hasan Abed tied workers' pay to what the mothers had actually learned.

story.event: Teaching mothers house by house to make oral rehydration solution, with pay tied to what they retained
story.summary: From 1980 BRAC's Oral Therapy Extension Programme sent teams of women door to door in rural Bangladesh to teach mothers to make oral rehydration solution from salt and gur. Fazle Hasan Abed had workers paid by how much mothers remembered when monitors returned, checked the monitors themselves, and published evaluations showing low use and slipping safety, which led BRAC to change its teaching; over about a decade the programme reached some 12 to 13 million households.
paragraphs: In 1980 teams of BRAC field workers set out on foot across rural Bangladesh. Each team, Atul Gawande later wrote, was fourteen young women, a cook and a male supervisor; they camped near a village and went door to door until they had spoken to the women in every home. The lesson came down to seven messages and a recipe measured by hand: a three-finger pinch of salt and a fistful of gur, raw sugar, in half a seer of water.

BRAC's founder, Fazle Hasan Abed, was an accountant who had worked for Shell; he had no training in public health. Oral rehydration had been proved in Dhaka a decade earlier, yet it had stalled. The World Health Organization doubted home-made mixtures, a solution with too much salt could harm a child, and there were nowhere near enough doctors. A 1979 trial had shown that illiterate mothers, taught by word of mouth, could make a solution that passed laboratory tests.

Abed's decision was to pay for learning rather than for visits. Monitors returned weeks after a lesson to quiz the mothers, and each worker's pay depended on how many of the messages they had kept. When checks showed teaching slipping at twenty households a day, the limit became ten. The checkers were checked too: to catch monitors "falsifying results from a tea stall", as Abed put it, workers privately recorded the name of each mother's youngest child for managers to compare. Thirty-seven monitors were dismissed. "Unless people are checked, they become sloppy," he said.

Not every finding was welcome. An evaluation Abed co-wrote, covering more than 7,000 households, found families used the solution in only about 5 to 10 per cent of diarrhoea episodes, though in a quarter to a half of severe ones, and that mothers' skill in making it safely slipped about six months after training. BRAC stressed the danger of excess salt and began teaching neighbours together. When anthropology students found husbands withholding support, workers explained the solution to men as well.

Over about ten years, with the government, the programme reached most of rural Bangladesh: "13 million households", Abed recalled, though other accounts count 12 million. Three decades on, national surveys found almost nine in ten children with severe diarrhoea were given the solution.

quote.text: For sheep do not hastily throw up the grass to show the shepherds how much they have eaten, but, inwardly digesting their food, they produce it outwardly in wool and milk.
quote.source_title: The Enchiridion, tr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Project Gutenberg eBook #45109
quote.connection: Epictetus wanted learning judged by what it produces, not by what can be recited on demand. BRAC came to the same test: workers were paid for what mothers could repeat, but the evaluations Abed published asked the harder question of whether sick children were actually given the drink.

reflection: Abed's programme could have counted visits and called that success. Instead it kept asking harder questions, and some answers were unwelcome: mothers forgot, mixtures drifted saltier, families did not use what they knew. The programme got better because it went on asking.

You teach people too, whether a new colleague learning a method or your family learning what your days involve. Recall is easy to check; use is not. The more honest test is to come back a few weeks later and see what has actually changed, then adjust the teaching rather than blame the learner.
invitation: Think of one thing you explained to someone in the past month. Ask them, without testing, how it has gone in practice, and listen for what your first explanation missed.

cross_checks.claim: From 1980 BRAC sent workers door to door to teach mothers to make oral rehydration solution at home
Workers were paid according to how much mothers retained when monitors followed up, and daily teaching was capped at ten
The recipe was a pinch of salt and a fistful of gur or sugar in about half a litre of water
Evaluations found many taught families did not use the solution, and BRAC changed its teaching, including bringing men into the discussions
Over about a decade the programme reached some 12 to 13 million households

research_notes: Reach, the main conflicting figure: Abed told PBS (2005) '13 million households' over ten years; Gawande (New Yorker, 2013) says twelve million families; Amy Yee (NYT, 2014) says more than 12 million women; a 2019 Daily Star tribute by Irene Khan says about 11.8 million homes, 98 per cent of rural households. The story gives Abed's figure as his recollection and notes that others count 12 million. BRAC's own 1988 papers give interim figures (over 5 million households; over a third of all households). Recipe: Gawande says a fistful of raw sugar and a three-finger pinch of salt in half a seer of water; Yee says a handful of sugar and half a litre; the 1988 papers call it lobon-gur (salt and unrefined sugar), and the World Health Forum paper says refined sugar was later promoted because gur is seasonal. The story says gur, raw sugar. Pilot sizes differ by stage (Gawande: a pilot aimed at about 60,000 women in 600 villages; Yee: a 1979 three-month trial and a second pilot of 9,000 women) and are not given. The ten-a-day cap: Gawande attributes it to monitors finding quality falling at twenty; Yee to the second pilot; the story follows Gawande. Usage: the IJE evaluation's 5-10 per cent overall and 25-52 per cent for severe diarrhoea or cholera are quoted from its abstract, as is the decline about six months after training; the story turns 25-52 per cent into 'a quarter to a half'. The men's finding comes from Yee's interview with Abed and PBS's account; its date is not given, so the story does not date it. The later figure of almost ninety per cent is Gawande's, for severe diarrhoea; Yee gives 78 per cent for all diarrhoea since 2007. The story does not credit BRAC alone with the national fall in child deaths, which PBS's profile appears to do. The 1988 papers, co-written by Abed, are listed as company-archive. Quote: Enchiridion 46 in Higginson's translation; applied by analogy to the gap between recall and use.
